newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan radio says UNITA on the move in north.
newsitem.headline: Angolan radio says UNITA on the move in north.

text.p: Angolan state radio on Sunday accused the former rebel movement UNITA of mobilising soldiers in the northern province of Uige, near the scene of renewed fighting that is threatening the country's fragile peace.
The radio quoted the vice-governor of defence for the province, Fernando Jose Kenge, as saying heavily armed UNITA troops had been seen in at least four areas in the province.
Kenge said the troops had reoccupied military bases abandoned under terms of a peace pact signed in 1994 between UNITA, led by Jonas Savimbi, and the government of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
The report could not be independently confirmed.

The 1994 treaty, backed by the United Nations, gave Angola its longest period of peace since civil war broke out on independence in 1975. The treaty led to the inauguration of a national unity government with UNITA's participation in April.

But fighting resumed three weeks ago in the northeastern province of Lunda Norte after Mobutu Sese Seko, one of UNITA's main backers, was ousted as president of neighbouring Zaire, now renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The country's new ruler, Laurent Kabila, is backed by the dos Santos government, which said it sent troops to the northern border with Kabila's Congo because of the danger of the conflict spilling into Angola.
But Western diplomats said the Angolan troops, taking advantage of the demobilisation of UNITA fighters, had sought to seize rich diamond areas controlled by Savimbi's men.
A U.N. spokesman in Angola, David Wimhurst, said on Saturday the United Nations had no evidence of heavy battles in the northeast.

U.N. military commander Phillip Sibanda visited the area on Friday and is due to return on Monday. The Angolan government has reported to him that 14 of its soldiers have been killed in skirmishes in the northeast.
A military source said on Saturday dos Santos's generals were reinforcing their troops in Lunda Norte and appeared determined to press deeper into UNITA-controlled territory.
The U.N. special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, has accused news media of exaggerating reports of fighting.

Under the 1994 peace agreement, the Angolan Armed Forces are supposed to remain in barracks until both the government and UNITA agree that conditions are right to lift restrictions on the movement of soldiers.
